description: Two-panel composite of tensile mechanical behaviour for the same low-density medium-Mn steel loaded along two directions; both panels use a red curve for "Rolling direction" and a blue curve for "Transverse direction" (legend printed in each panel). (a) Engineering Stress (MPa, ticks 100-900, 100 MPa intervals) vs Engineering Strain (%, ticks 0-80, 10 % intervals). Both curves show a sharp elastic rise then continuous hardening; the red (RD) curve reaches higher stress and larger strain before a sudden load drop, and both fracture points carry horizontal error bars (red fatigue/ductility scatter spanning roughly 70-75 % strain at ~740 MPa; blue scatter ~63-68 % at ~810 MPa). (b) Dual-quantity plot with Strain Hardening Rate (dσ/dε) and True Stress on one MPa axis (500-2500) against True Strain (0.0-0.5): the upper pair of curves is the hardening rate, the lower near-linear pair is true stress rising to ~1400 MPa. Three colour-shaded regimes are labelled Stage I (sharp drop), Stage II (hardening-rate rise from ~0.2 true strain), and Stage III (decline), with a red/blue double-headed arrow marking Stage II and an upward arrow near 0.43 true strain. Overall: the RD sample hardens faster at high strain, giving the higher strength and ductility of panel (a).

observations.observation: Panel (a) plots engineering stress (MPa) against engineering strain (%) with two curves labelled in the legend as 'Rolling direction' (red) and 'Transverse direction' (blue).

In panel (a) the rolling-direction curve reaches the higher peak stress and the larger strain before fracture, whereas the transverse-direction curve terminates earlier at a slightly lower stress; horizontal error bars are drawn at each fracture point.
The caption states panel (a) shows the engineering stress-strain curves of the two samples and panel (b) their corresponding strain hardening curves and true stress-strain curves.
The citing text reports a tensile strength of approximately 855±35 MPa and total elongation of 65±5 % for the intercritically annealed steel tested at room temperature.
The citing text states the RD sample has higher strength (by 864 MPa) and higher ductility (69 %) than the TD sample.
Panel (b) uses a single MPa axis for two quantities, labelled 'Strain Hardening Rate (dσ/dε) & True Stress (MPa)', against True Strain from 0.0 to 0.5.
Panel (b) is divided into three colour-shaded regions labelled Stage I, Stage II and Stage III, with a vertical boundary near 0.2 true strain separating Stage I from Stage II.

The citing text describes Stage I as a sharp drop in strain-hardening rate, Stage II as an increase starting from a true strain of ~0.2 for both samples, and Stage III as a renewed decrease until necking defined by the Considère criterion.
The citing text reports the maximum strain-hardening rate of the RD sample as 2052 MPa versus 1828 MPa for the TD sample.
An upward arrow is drawn at the transition from Stage II to Stage III on the red rolling-direction hardening curve in panel (b), at roughly 0.43 true strain.
The true stress-strain curves in panel (b) rise almost linearly from the Stage I region and reach approximately 1400 MPa at the end of the test.
The citing text states that an engineering stress-strain curve acquired from an in-situ HEXRD tensile stage is also shown in Fig. 4(a).

subfigures.description: Engineering stress-strain curves, axes 'Engineering Stress (MPa)' (100-900) vs 'Engineering Strain (%)' (0-80). Red = Rolling direction, blue = Transverse direction. Both curves rise steeply then harden smoothly; the red curve peaks at a higher stress and strains further before a sudden drop, and error bars are plotted at the final fracture points of both curves.

Plot of 'Strain Hardening Rate (dσ/dε) & True Stress (MPa)' (500-2500) vs 'True Strain' (0.0-0.5), red = Rolling direction, blue = Transverse direction. Upper curves are strain-hardening rate with three shaded and labelled regimes: Stage I (steep initial drop), Stage II (rise beginning near 0.2 true strain, marked by a double arrow), Stage III (decreasing hardening rate); the lower pair of nearly straight, slowly rising curves is the true stress-strain response reaching ~1400 MPa.
